deck.topic: Low appraisal and the gap clause most buyers sign blind
deck.hook: Appraisal came in $14,000 short. Seller kept every dollar.

points.title: The Appraisal Is Not Yours
body: You pay for it. The lender orders it and owns the result.
It exists to protect the loan amount, not the price you agreed to.

points.title: Low Value Is Not A Discount
body: The lender funds off the appraised number. Your contract price stays exactly where it was.
Nothing about a low appraisal automatically lowers what you owe the seller.

points.title: Where The $14,000 Went
body: That buyer had signed an appraisal gap clause agreeing to cover a shortfall in cash.
So the price never moved. The $14,000 came straight out of their savings at closing.

points.title: Cap It, Do Not Waive It
body: Waiving means you cover any shortfall, however big it turns out to be.
Capping sets a ceiling you pick. It still beats most competing offers.
points.loop: Ceiling is not the only lever.

points.title: The Clock You Missed
body: In Texas the right to walk after a low appraisal lives on its own addendum with its own deadline.
Blow past that date and your earnest money quietly stops being yours.
points.loop: You can size this risk early.

linkedinCaption:
An appraisal comes back low and most buyers assume the price drops. It does not. The lender funds off the appraised value. Your contract price stays where you signed it, and the difference becomes cash you bring to closing.

One buyer brought $14,000. They had signed an appraisal gap clause months earlier without reading it closely.

The slides below cover who the appraisal actually protects, why capping a gap beats waiving it, and the Texas addendum deadline that quietly ends your right to walk.

Most of this is fixable at the offer stage. Very little of it is fixable at the closing table.

For the agents here: how are you explaining gap coverage to first time buyers in a competitive offer?
